source.variation: GNPS's children's Punjabi app (Apache-2.0; developer CodeManX) has a tracing lesson whose checkpoints the developer entered over the Noto Sans Gurmukhi letter, one list per pen-down stroke, and whose trace widget makes the child reach them in order. It writes ਟ in two pen-down strokes: the headline from left to right; then from the top right down the short stem, left and down the left side, and round the base to the bottom right. The headline first is the source's teaching order. Fluent writers are often described as adding the headline last (Alfaazo's general guidance on Gurmukhi; native Devanagari writers do so in HP Labs India's pen data), so the path shows how this lesson teaches the letter, not how every fluent hand writes it. Omniglot (Lake, Salakhutdinov & Tenenbaum, Science 350:1332, 2015; https://github.com/brendenlake/omniglot, MIT licence) holds 20 drawings of ਟ, each by a different non-native copyist; only counts and shares are cited. 90% (18 of 20) draw it in two strokes, the source's count and their most common one. For the first stroke of the body, 65% (13 of 20) start in the same part of the letter as the source and 100% (20 of 20) set off in the same direction, within 45 degrees. Only the order, the start, the direction and the lifts are taken from the source; no checkpoint coordinate is copied, and the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Gurmukhi outline. Handwriting varies by writer.

source.variation: GNPS's children's Punjabi app (Apache-2.0; developer CodeManX) has a tracing lesson whose checkpoints the developer entered over the Noto Sans Gurmukhi letter, one list per pen-down stroke, and whose trace widget makes the child reach them in order. It writes ਰ in two pen-down strokes: the headline from left to right; then from the top right down the stem, clockwise round the bowl and right along the bar, ending at the stem. The headline first is the source's teaching order. Fluent writers are often described as adding the headline last (Alfaazo's general guidance on Gurmukhi; native Devanagari writers do so in HP Labs India's pen data), so the path shows how this lesson teaches the letter, not how every fluent hand writes it. Omniglot (Lake, Salakhutdinov & Tenenbaum, Science 350:1332, 2015; https://github.com/brendenlake/omniglot, MIT licence) holds 20 drawings of ਰ, each by a different non-native copyist; only counts and shares are cited. 100% (20 of 20) draw it in two strokes, the source's count and their most common one. For the first stroke of the body, 65% (13 of 20) start in the same part of the letter as the source and 100% (20 of 20) set off in the same direction, within 45 degrees. Only the order, the start, the direction and the lifts are taken from the source; no checkpoint coordinate is copied, and the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Gurmukhi outline. Handwriting varies by writer.

source.citation: GNPS, Gurmukhi Sikho (GNPS Learning Hub), Alphabet Tracing lesson, ੜ (rhaarhaa) checkpoints, strokes 1–3 (lib/data/lessons/lesson_tracing.dart line 1108, commit de1e560; Apache-2.0)
source.variation: GNPS's children's Punjabi app (Apache-2.0; developer CodeManX) has a tracing lesson whose checkpoints the developer entered over the Noto Sans Gurmukhi letter, one list per pen-down stroke, and whose trace widget makes the child reach them in order. It writes ੜ in three pen-down strokes: the headline from left to right; then from the top right down to the left, clockwise round the knob and the right side, and left along the base to the bottom left; then the short right leg, down to the right. The headline first is the source's teaching order. Fluent writers are often described as adding the headline last (Alfaazo's general guidance on Gurmukhi; native Devanagari writers do so in HP Labs India's pen data), so the path shows how this lesson teaches the letter, not how every fluent hand writes it. The outline prints the knob as a solid teardrop, so the path loops clockwise inside it. Omniglot (Lake, Salakhutdinov & Tenenbaum, Science 350:1332, 2015; https://github.com/brendenlake/omniglot, MIT licence) holds 20 drawings of ੜ, each by a different non-native copyist; only counts and shares are cited. 65% (13 of 20) draw it in three strokes, the source's count and their most common one. For the first stroke of the body, 70% (14 of 20) start in the same part of the letter as the source and 85% (17 of 20) set off in the same direction, within 45 degrees. Only the order, the start, the direction and the lifts are taken from the source; no checkpoint coordinate is copied, and the path is fitted to the bundled Noto Sans Gurmukhi outline. Handwriting varies by writer.
